title: Chemical formulas: how H₂O, CO₂ and NaCl say which atoms and how many

summary.text: Salt is called uppu in Chennai, namak in Delhi and nun in Kolkata. A chemist in any of these cities writes it as NaCl. A chemical formula uses letters to say which atoms are in a substance. It uses small numbers to say how many. Water is H₂O: two hydrogen atoms for each oxygen atom. People chose the letters, but they had to measure to find the numbers. Your child counts drops of iodine to see that substances react in fixed amounts. They also build water, carbon dioxide and a grain of salt from balls of dough.
summary.art: Three small bowls of white salt with paper labels reading uppu, namak and nun, and one larger card behind them that reads NaCl.

intro.hook: The symbol for hydrogen is H, and the symbol for oxygen is O. So why is the symbol for sodium Na? The word sodium has neither an N nor an A in it.
intro.text: Chemists write every substance with a short code called a formula. Water is H₂O. Carbon dioxide, the gas you breathe out, is CO₂. Table salt is NaCl. The letters stand for kinds of atoms, and some of them come from old Latin names. Sodium was called natrium, so its symbol is Na. The small numbers say how many atoms there are. In this unit you collect the many names of one substance. You count drops of iodine to find out why the numbers are fixed. You also build molecules from dough and read the formulas of things in your kitchen.
intro.art: A child looking at a salt jar, a steel tumbler of water and a fizzing glass of soda, each with a small card in front: NaCl, H₂O and CO₂.

outcomes: I can read a chemical symbol and say which element it stands for.
I can read a formula such as H₂O, CO₂ or NaCl and say which atoms it has and how many.
I can explain why one atom more or one atom less makes a different substance.
I can explain that the formula of salt gives a ratio, because salt is a crystal with no separate molecules.
I can explain why the numbers in a formula are fixed, using my own drop counts.
I can tell apart a substance's everyday names, its chemical name and its formula.
I can say what a formula leaves out, and what it tells me a substance can never give.
I can say which part of a formula people agreed on and which part they had to measure.

terms.meaning: One of the tiny particles that every substance is made of. Atoms are far too small to see.
terms.example: A single drop of water holds more than a thousand million million million atoms.
terms.art: A drop of water with a magnifying circle beside it showing many tiny round balls.

terms.meaning: A substance made of only one kind of atom. 118 elements are known, and about 90 of them are found in nature.
terms.example: Gold is an element. Every atom in a pure gold ring is a gold atom.
terms.art: A gold ring with a magnifying circle showing identical balls packed together.

terms.meaning: One or two letters that stand for an element. The first letter is a capital, and the second letter is small.
terms.example: O stands for oxygen, C stands for carbon and Na stands for sodium.
terms.art: Three cards in a row reading O, C and Na, with the element names written small underneath.

terms.meaning: A short code for a substance. Its symbols say which atoms are in the substance, and its small numbers say how many.
terms.example: The formula H₂O says that water has two hydrogen atoms for each oxygen atom.
terms.art: The formula H₂O written large, with an arrow from each part to a small drawing of the atoms it stands for.

terms.meaning: The small number written low after a symbol in a formula. It says how many atoms of that element there are. No number means one atom.
terms.example: In CO₂ the small 2 belongs to the O. There are two oxygen atoms and one carbon atom.
terms.art: The formula CO₂ with the small 2 circled and an arrow from it to two red balls.

terms.meaning: A group of atoms joined together. A molecule is the smallest piece of many substances.
terms.example: One molecule of water is two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen atom.
terms.art: One large ball joined to two small balls in a wide V shape.

terms.meaning: A substance made of two or more elements joined in fixed numbers.
terms.example: Water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen. Salt is a compound of sodium and chlorine.
terms.art: Two different kinds of balls joined into a group, beside a jar of each kind of ball on its own.

terms.meaning: The lightest element. As a gas, its atoms come joined in pairs, written H₂.
terms.example: Every water molecule holds two hydrogen atoms.
terms.art: Two small white balls joined as a pair, labelled H₂.

terms.meaning: The element in air that humans and other animals need to breathe. In air, its atoms come joined in pairs, written O₂.
terms.example: About one fifth of the air in your room is oxygen gas.
terms.art: Two red balls joined as a pair, labelled O₂, drawn inside an outline of a pair of lungs.

terms.meaning: The element in charcoal, pencil lead and diamond. Carbon atoms are in every living body.
terms.example: The black tip of a burnt matchstick is mostly carbon.
terms.art: A burnt matchstick, a pencil and a diamond in a row, each labelled C.

terms.meaning: A soft, silvery metal that reacts fiercely with water. Its symbol comes from its old Latin name, natrium.
terms.example: Sodium is never found alone in a kitchen. It is joined to chlorine in salt.
terms.art: A small lump of soft silvery metal under oil in a glass jar, labelled Na.

terms.meaning: A yellow-green, poisonous gas when it is alone. Joined to sodium, it makes table salt.
terms.example: A tiny amount of chlorine is added to city tap water to kill microbes.
terms.art: A sealed glass flask of pale yellow-green gas, labelled Cl₂.

terms.meaning: A gas with one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms in each molecule. You breathe it out, and plants take it in.
terms.example: The bubbles in a bottle of soda are carbon dioxide.
terms.art: A glass of soda with rising bubbles, and one bubble enlarged to show a black ball between two red balls.

terms.meaning: The chemical name of table salt. It has one sodium atom for every chlorine atom.
terms.example: The salt in the sea, in rock salt and in a pickle jar is all sodium chloride.
terms.art: A heap of salt beside one enlarged cube-shaped grain.

terms.meaning: A way to say how many of one thing there are for each of another.
terms.example: In water the ratio is two hydrogen atoms to one oxygen atom. In salt it is one to one.
terms.art: Two small balls beside one large ball, with the words 2 to 1 written underneath.

terms.meaning: A name that chemists everywhere have agreed on. It says which elements are in the substance.
terms.example: Baking soda, cooking soda and meetha soda are everyday names. Sodium hydrogen carbonate is the chemical name.
terms.art: A packet of baking soda turned to show the small print on the back, with one line underlined.

terms.meaning: A solid whose atoms are packed in a pattern that repeats in every direction.
terms.example: A grain of salt is a crystal. Its sodium and chlorine atoms sit in rows, one after the other.
terms.art: A cube built of two colours of balls that alternate like a chessboard.

terms.meaning: Different substances that have the same formula. The same atoms are joined in a different arrangement.
terms.example: Glucose and fructose are two sugars. Both have the formula C₆H₁₂O₆.
terms.art: Two different shapes built from the same set of coloured balls, side by side.

explanations.concept: A symbol is one or two letters for one element
explanations.definition: A chemical symbol is one or two letters that stand for an element. The first letter is always a capital, and a second letter is always small.
explanations.description: An element is a substance made of only one kind of atom. Each element has its own symbol. Many symbols are the first letter of the English name: H for hydrogen, O for oxygen, C for carbon. There are 118 elements and only 26 letters, so most symbols need a second letter. Chlorine is Cl and calcium is Ca. Some symbols come from old Latin names. Sodium was natrium, so it is Na. Iron was ferrum, so it is Fe. Gold was aurum, so it is Au. The rule about capitals matters. Co is one atom of the metal cobalt. CO is two atoms, carbon and oxygen, joined as a poisonous gas. The symbols are the same in every country and every language.
examples: K is potassium, from the Latin name kalium. The K on a fertiliser bag marked NPK is potassium.
Ag is silver, from argentum. Cu is copper, from cuprum.
No element's symbol uses the letter J or the letter Q.
explanations.art: A row of element cards reading H, O, C, Na, Fe and Au, each with its English name and its old Latin name underneath.

explanations.concept: A formula says which atoms and how many
explanations.definition: A chemical formula is a short code for a substance. The symbols say which kinds of atoms are in it. A small number after a symbol says how many of that atom there are.
explanations.description: Read a formula from left to right, one symbol at a time. A small number, called a subscript, belongs to the symbol just before it. If a symbol has no number, there is one atom. H₂O has two symbols, H and O. The small 2 comes after the H, so there are two hydrogen atoms. The O has no number, so there is one oxygen atom. One water molecule has three atoms in all. CO₂ has one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms. A formula is the same wherever the substance comes from. Water from the Kaveri, from a cloud and from your tap is H₂O.
examples: H₂O is water: 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom.
CO₂ is carbon dioxide: 1 carbon atom and 2 oxygen atoms.
CH₄ is methane, the main gas in CNG: 1 carbon atom and 4 hydrogen atoms.
explanations.art: The formula H₂O with a line from the H and the small 2 to two small white balls, and a line from the O to one red ball.

explanations.definition: An element's formula shows how its atoms come. Some come as single atoms, and some come joined in pairs or in larger groups.
explanations.description: Oxygen gas is written O₂, because its atoms come joined in pairs. The nitrogen in air is N₂, and hydrogen gas is H₂. Their molecules hold two atoms of the same kind. So a molecule does not have to be a compound. A metal such as gold has no molecules. Its atoms are packed together in one big crystal, so its formula is just Au. The air in your room is mostly two formulas. About four fifths of it is N₂, and about one fifth is O₂. Carbon dioxide is only about 4 molecules in every 10,000.
examples: O₂ is the oxygen you breathe: 2 oxygen atoms.
N₂ is nitrogen gas: 2 nitrogen atoms.
Fe is iron and Au is gold. A metal is written with its symbol alone.
explanations.art: A room with a child in it, and three kinds of small molecule floating: many blue pairs, fewer red pairs, and one black ball with two red balls.

explanations.concept: One atom more makes a different substance
explanations.definition: Two substances can be made of the same elements and still be different. If the numbers in their formulas differ, they are different substances.
explanations.description: Water is H₂O. Hydrogen peroxide is H₂O₂. It has one more oxygen atom in each molecule. Water is safe to drink. Hydrogen peroxide bleaches hair and kills microbes on a cut. Carbon dioxide is CO₂, and you breathe it out all day. Carbon monoxide is CO, with one oxygen atom fewer. It forms when fuel burns without enough air, and it is a deadly poison. Oxygen gas is O₂. Ozone is O₃, and it has a sharp smell and harms the lungs. So every number in a formula matters. Changing one small number gives a different substance with different behaviour.
examples: H₂O is water. H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide.
CO₂ is carbon dioxide. CO is carbon monoxide.
O₂ is the oxygen in air. O₃ is ozone, which blocks harmful rays high above the Earth.
explanations.art: Two pairs of molecule drawings side by side: water beside hydrogen peroxide, and carbon dioxide beside carbon monoxide, with the extra atom in each pair circled.

explanations.concept: The formula of salt gives a ratio
explanations.definition: Salt has no separate molecules. Its formula, NaCl, says that there is one sodium atom for every chlorine atom.
explanations.description: A grain of salt is a crystal. Its sodium and chlorine atoms are packed in rows that alternate, like the squares of a chessboard, in every direction. Each sodium atom has chlorine atoms on all six sides. No sodium atom belongs to one chlorine atom more than to the others. So there is no small piece that you could call one molecule of salt. The formula gives the ratio. For every sodium atom in the grain there is one chlorine atom. One grain holds about a million million million atoms. The atoms in salt carry electric charges, and chemists call such charged atoms ions. You will meet ions in a later unit.
examples: NaCl is table salt: 1 sodium for every 1 chlorine.
CaCO₃ is the substance of chalk, marble and eggshell: 1 calcium and 1 carbon for every 3 oxygen.
SiO₂ is quartz, the main part of most sand: 1 silicon for every 2 oxygen.
explanations.art: A cube-shaped salt grain, and beside it an enlarged corner showing two colours of balls alternating in rows.

explanations.concept: Why the numbers in a formula are fixed
explanations.definition: Atoms join and react in fixed whole numbers. So a pure compound always has the same proportions, wherever it comes from.
explanations.description: An atom cannot join with half of another atom. Atoms join one to one, one to two, two to three, and so on. In the experiment Count the Drops, you can see this at work. Lemon juice holds vitamin C. One molecule of vitamin C changes exactly one molecule of iodine and takes away its colour. So twice as much lemon juice uses up about twice as many drops of iodine. In 1799 the French chemist Joseph Proust showed the same thing by weighing. A copper compound from a mine and the same compound made in his laboratory had the same proportions. Fixed proportions were the first strong clue that substances are made of atoms.
examples: Water always has 2 hydrogen atoms for each oxygen atom.
Twice the lemon juice uses up about twice the iodine.
A cook can change the amounts in a recipe and still make a dish. A pure compound has only one set of amounts, and it can never change.
explanations.art: Two glasses of pale liquid, the second holding twice as much lemon juice, with eight drops falling into the first and sixteen into the second.

explanations.concept: Everyday names, chemical names and formulas
explanations.definition: An everyday name is what people call a substance at home. A chemical name says which elements are in it. A formula also says how many atoms of each.
explanations.description: One substance can have hundreds of everyday names, one in each language. Salt is uppu, namak, nun and salt. An everyday name tells you nothing about what the substance is made of. A chemical name does. Sodium chloride holds sodium and chlorine. When a metal joins a non-metal, the metal is named first and the other name ends in ide. Small words inside a name count atoms. Mono means one, di means two and tri means three. So carbon dioxide has two oxygen atoms and carbon monoxide has one. In 1787 four French chemists, among them Antoine Lavoisier, proposed naming substances by what they are made of. Since 1919 a world body of chemists called IUPAC has agreed the rules.
examples: Everyday name: baking soda. Chemical name: sodium hydrogen carbonate. Formula: NaHCO₃.
Everyday name: dry ice. Chemical name: solid carbon dioxide. Formula: CO₂.
Everyday name: chalk. Chemical name: calcium carbonate. Formula: CaCO₃.
explanations.art: A packet of baking soda with three labels beside it: an everyday name, a chemical name and a formula.

explanations.concept: A formula shows what a substance can never give
explanations.definition: A chemical change rearranges atoms. It cannot make a new kind of atom. So a substance heated alone can give off only what its own atoms can build.
explanations.description: Salt and baking soda are both dry white powders. Salt is NaCl. Baking soda is NaHCO₃, so it holds hydrogen, carbon and oxygen atoms as well as sodium. Water is H₂O and carbon dioxide is CO₂. Baking soda has the atoms to build both. Salt has the atoms for neither. In the experiment Water from a Dry Powder, a grown-up heats each powder. Baking soda gives off water, which wets a cold steel plate. Salt gives off none. No water was hiding in the baking soda. Heat rearranged its atoms into three new substances: water, carbon dioxide and washing soda.
examples: Heated baking soda gives off water and carbon dioxide.
Heated salt gives off neither, because it has no hydrogen, carbon or oxygen atoms.
No amount of heating turns iron atoms into gold atoms.
explanations.art: Two small pans on a stove, one with a cold steel plate above it covered in tiny drops, and the other with a plate that is dry.

explanations.definition: A formula says which atoms and how many. It does not say how the atoms are arranged.
explanations.description: Glucose is the sugar in your blood. Fructose is a sugar in fruit and honey. Both have the formula C₆H₁₂O₆. Each molecule has 6 carbon, 12 hydrogen and 6 oxygen atoms. But the atoms are joined in a different arrangement, so the two sugars are different substances. Fructose tastes sweeter. Substances like these are called isomers. To know a substance fully, chemists must also find its arrangement. The British chemist Dorothy Hodgkin did this with X-rays. She worked out the arrangement of the atoms in penicillin in 1945 and in vitamin B12 in the 1950s. Vitamin B12 has 181 atoms in each molecule.
examples: Glucose and fructose are both C₆H₁₂O₆, and they are different sugars.
Diamond and pencil lead are both written C, and they are arranged differently.
The formula of vitamin B12 is C₆₃H₈₈CoN₁₄O₁₄P. It took years of work to find how those atoms are joined.
explanations.art: Two different ball-and-stick shapes built from the same set of balls, with the same formula written under each.

explanations.concept: Formulas in living bodies, on the Earth and in space
explanations.definition: The same symbols can write every substance yet found, in a living body, in a rock or between the stars.
explanations.description: About 99 of every 100 atoms in your body are of just four kinds: hydrogen, oxygen, carbon and nitrogen. A plant takes in CO₂ and H₂O and builds glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆. You eat the glucose and breathe out CO₂ and H₂O again. Astronomers can tell which substances are far away, because each substance takes in its own colours of light. The air of Venus and of Mars is mostly CO₂. In 2009 an instrument on India's Chandrayaan-1 spacecraft found signs of water on the Moon. In 1969 radio telescopes found water molecules in clouds between the stars. In 2022 the James Webb Space Telescope found CO₂ in the air of a planet that orbits another star.
examples: Photosynthesis in words: carbon dioxide and water become glucose and oxygen.
The air of Mars is about 95 parts CO₂ in every 100.
Water in a comet has the same formula as water in a coconut: H₂O.
explanations.art: A child, a mango tree, the Moon and a distant planet in one picture, each tagged with a small label reading H₂O or CO₂.

explanations.concept: Is a formula a fact about nature, or a tool that people made?
explanations.definition: Chemists agree on how to write and use formulas. People who study science disagree about what a formula really is.
explanations.description: A formula has two parts. The letters were chosen by people, and they could have been different. The numbers were found by measuring, and nobody could choose them. So is the whole formula a fact, or a tool?
examples: H was chosen for hydrogen. In a different history it might have been a picture or another letter.
Some early chemists wrote water as HO. Measurements showed that the 2 was needed, so they had to give up HO and write H₂O.

perspectives.explanation: A formula is a fact about nature, written in agreed symbols. Water really has two hydrogen atoms for each oxygen atom. Any careful person who measures will find the same.

perspectives.who: Ernst Mach and Wilhelm Ostwald, two scientists of about 1900
perspectives.explanation: A formula is a tool for keeping track of measurements. It should not be taken as a picture of hidden things. Ostwald changed his mind a few years later, after experiments made the case for atoms much stronger.
Both are partly right. A formula is a human way of writing, and what it writes down is real. It also leaves out a great deal, such as the arrangement of the atoms.

explanations.art: The formula H₂O drawn twice: once carved into a rock, and once written on a slate held by a person.

agreed.text: Every substance is made of atoms, and a formula lists which kinds and how many.
agreed.evidence: Chemists can take a compound apart, weigh each element in it, and build the same compound again from those elements.

agreed.text: Water has two hydrogen atoms for each oxygen atom.
agreed.evidence: In 1805 Gay-Lussac and Humboldt measured the gases that join to make water. Hydrogen took up twice as much space as oxygen.

agreed.text: A pure compound has the same proportions wherever it comes from.
agreed.evidence: In 1799 Joseph Proust compared a copper compound from a mine with the same compound made in his laboratory. The proportions were the same.

agreed.text: Salt is a crystal of sodium and chlorine atoms in equal numbers. It has no separate molecules.
agreed.evidence: In 1913 William Lawrence Bragg used X-rays to find where the atoms sit in a salt crystal. Each sodium atom has six chlorine atoms around it.

agreed.text: Two different substances can have the same formula.
agreed.evidence: In the 1820s Friedrich Wöhler and Justus von Liebig each analysed a silver compound. One was harmless and one exploded, yet both had the same atoms in the same numbers.

agreed.text: Chemists in every country use the same symbols and the same rules for names.
agreed.evidence: Since 1919 a world body of chemists, called IUPAC, has agreed the symbols and names. It also approves the name of each new element.

challenging.claim: Water is HO: one hydrogen atom joined to one oxygen atom.
challenging.for: It is the simplest way that two kinds of atoms could join. Dalton had no way to count atoms directly.
challenging.against: When water is split, the hydrogen gas takes up twice the space of the oxygen gas. Avogadro's idea, accepted after 1860, explains this only if water is H₂O.

challenging.claim: Salt is made of tiny NaCl molecules.
challenging.who: A common belief, and a fair first reading of the formula.
challenging.for: Water is made of H₂O molecules, so it seems that salt should be made of NaCl molecules.
challenging.against: X-rays show that salt is one large pattern of sodium and chlorine atoms. Each sodium has six chlorine neighbours and belongs to none of them more than the others. The formula gives the ratio.

challenging.claim: The proportions in a compound can vary, as they do in a mixture.
challenging.who: Claude Louis Berthollet, a French chemist, in about 1803.
challenging.for: Mixtures such as salt water and alloys such as brass can be made in many proportions. In the 1900s chemists found a few solids whose proportions do vary slightly. One is an iron oxide called wüstite.
challenging.against: Proust showed that pure compounds such as water and salt always have the same proportions. This is true of nearly all compounds.

challenging.claim: A chemical is something made in a factory. Natural things are chemical-free.
challenging.who: A common belief, and many advertisements.
challenging.for: Many harmful substances are made in factories, so people use the word chemical to mean something harmful.
challenging.against: Everything made of atoms is a chemical. Water is H₂O, salt is NaCl and the sugar in a mango is C₆H₁₂O₆. Whether a substance harms you depends on which substance it is and how much you take.

challenging.claim: Vitamin C from amla is a different substance from vitamin C made in a factory.
challenging.for: Amla also brings fibre, water and many other substances that a tablet does not have.
challenging.against: The vitamin C molecule in both is C₆H₈O₆, with the same arrangement of atoms. The body cannot tell the two apart. Only the other substances that come along with it differ.

challenging.claim: If you know the formula, you know the substance.
challenging.who: A common belief among people who have just learned formulas.
challenging.for: A formula does tell you a lot: which atoms, how many, and what the substance can never give off.
challenging.against: Glucose and fructose share the formula C₆H₁₂O₆ and are different sugars. Diamond and pencil lead are both C. The arrangement of the atoms matters as much as the count.

challenging.claim: Pictures would make better symbols than letters.
challenging.who: John Dalton, who kept his circles and disliked the letters of Berzelius.
challenging.for: A picture can show how the atoms sit beside each other, which a row of letters does not show.
challenging.against: Letters can be written and printed quickly by anyone. Chemists chose letters for everyday work. They do use pictures of molecules when the arrangement matters, so Dalton was partly right.

big_questions.q: People chose the letter H for hydrogen. Could they also have chosen the number in H₂O?
big_questions.hint: Think about Count the Drops. Could you have chosen how many drops the lemon juice used up?

big_questions.q: Water has thousands of names and one formula. Is any of them its real name?
big_questions.hint: Was water any different before people had a word for it?

big_questions.q: One molecule of H₂O is not wet and cannot be poured. How many molecules does it take to make water?
big_questions.hint: Think of a heap of sand. One grain is not a heap, and neither are two. Somewhere between a few grains and a lot, it becomes a heap. Is water like that?

big_questions.q: Glucose and fructose have the same formula and are different sugars. What else might a formula be leaving out?
big_questions.hint: A list of the people in a family does not say who is whose mother.

big_questions.q: Of 118 elements, only two are named after women: curium and meitnerium. Who gets to name things, and is that fair?
big_questions.hint: Curium honours Marie and Pierre Curie. Meitnerium honours Lise Meitner. Who decided on the other names?

big_questions.q: The same symbols write a rock, a river, a mango and you. Does that make you more like a rock than you thought?
big_questions.hint: About 99 of every 100 atoms in your body are hydrogen, oxygen, carbon or nitrogen.

big_questions.q: Children in every country learn the same chemical symbols. What else would be easier if the whole world wrote it the same way?
big_questions.hint: Think about numbers, music notes and road signs. Which of them are written the same way in every country?

story.title: The Sack with the H
story.note: Yazhini, Kokila Periamma, Nila Akka, Bablu and the shop are made up. These facts are real. Burrabazar is a large wholesale market in Kolkata. Bengali letters hang from a line along the top. Many Tamil speakers call baking soda soda uppu, and many Bengali speakers call it khabar soda. Nun is a Bengali word for salt. Baking soda is NaHCO₃. Washing soda, also sold as soda ash, is Na₂CO₃. Factory sacks usually print the chemical name. Only some of them print the formula as well.
text: Yazhini had been in Kolkata for one day, and she could not read any of it.

The shop boards were in Bengali. The letters were round, and they hung from a line, like washing from a rope. The bus boards were the same. At home in Madurai she read everything, even the backs of biscuit packets. Here she read nothing.

She had come with Kokila Periamma, her mother's elder sister, who cooked for weddings. A Tamil family in Kolkata wanted a Madurai cook for their daughter's wedding. Tomorrow evening four hundred guests would eat vazhaikkai bajji, hot from the oil.
That morning Periamma turned a steel tin upside down over her palm. A little white dust fell out.
"Soda uppu," she said. "I packed the empty tin. Without it the bajji will be as hard as chappals. Go to the big market with the driver, kanna. Bring half a kilo."
"How will I ask? I don't know Bengali."
"Uppu is uppu," said Periamma. She believed that everybody understood Tamil if you said it slowly.
Yazhini put the empty tin in her cloth bag, to show the shopkeeper. On its lid, in red nail polish, somebody had painted NaHCO₃.

That was her sister's work. Nila Akka was in her first year of chemistry at college. She had painted a formula on every jar in the kitchen, and H₂O on the cat's water bowl. "It is only a list," Akka had said. "Na is sodium. H is hydrogen. C is carbon. O is oxygen, and the small 3 says there are three of them. Read it like a shopping list." Yazhini had not been very interested.
The market was called Burrabazar. The driver stopped at a shop with open sacks along its front. Yazhini counted nine sacks. Every one of them held a white powder.
A boy of about twelve came out with a steel scoop. The driver called him Bablu.
"Soda uppu," said Yazhini slowly.
"Soda?" Bablu dug into the third sack and held out a scoop.

Yazhini rubbed a pinch between her fingers. Periamma's soda uppu was as soft as flour. This powder was gritty. Bablu rubbed his fists together, as if he were scrubbing a shirt. It was a soda for washing clothes.
"Uppu," Yazhini tried. She pretended to sprinkle something over food.
"Nun!" said Bablu. He ran to the first sack and came back with a handful of salt.

So now there was a soda that was not hers, and an uppu that was not hers. The right powder was somewhere among seven more sacks. On each sack stood a small slate with its name in chalk, in round letters that hung from a line.
She looked at the sacks themselves. Under the dust, each one had words stamped on it by the factory, in small black print. She bent down to the washing soda.
SODA ASH, it said. Under that: Na₂CO₃.
Her stomach jumped. She knew that row of marks, or nearly. She took the tin out of her bag and held the lid beside the stamp.
Na. Both began the same way. Then the sack had a small 2, and the lid had none. Then the lid had an H, and the sack had none. Both ended with CO₃.
Two sodiums and no hydrogen, she thought. It is a different list, so it is a different powder.

She walked along the row and read every stamp. NaCl was the salt. The second sack said CaCO₃, and the fourth said C₆H₁₂O₆. She did not know what those were, and she did not need to know. They were not her list.
The seventh sack said NaHCO₃.
She checked it against the lid, mark by mark, with her finger. One sodium. One hydrogen. One carbon. Three oxygens. Nothing was extra, and nothing was missing.
It was the first thing in Kolkata she had been able to read.
"This one," she said. She held the lid against the stamp for Bablu.
He looked from one to the other. He put his finger on the H on the lid, and then on the H on the sack. He laughed.
"Khabar soda!" he said.
"Soda uppu," said Yazhini.
"Khabar soda."
"Soda uppu."
Each of them pointed at the same sack and laughed. Bablu weighed out half a kilo.

Then he picked up the chalk. Under the round letters on the slate, he began to copy the marks from the lid. He drew the 3 as tall as the letters. Yazhini shook her head. She rubbed it out with her thumb and wrote it small and low.
"Three oxygens," she said in Tamil, and held up three fingers.
Bablu held up three fingers too.
At the wedding house, Periamma rubbed a pinch of the powder between her fingers. It was as soft as flour.
"Soda uppu," she said. "I told you. Uppu is uppu."
Yazhini said nothing. On the drive back she had been looking out of the window for more. She had found one, on the side of a truck that carried gas cylinders.
"CO₂," she had told the driver. "One carbon and two oxygens."
The driver did not know Tamil either. He had nodded kindly, and driven on.
story.epiphany: Soda uppu, khabar soda and soda were three names, and they did not tell Yazhini which sack to choose. The formula on the sack listed the atoms and how many of each. By checking that list mark by mark, she found the one powder that matched her tin.
ask: Two sacks were both called soda. How do the formulas Na₂CO₃ and NaHCO₃ differ?
Bablu drew the 3 as tall as the letters. Why does it matter that the 3 is small and low?
Which words on a packet at your home could a child in another country read?

games.title: Read It Out: the formula cards
games.context: This is a card game about reading formulas. Each card shows a formula. You say which atoms it has and how many, and then you name the substance.

setup.art: Twenty small cards in a shuffled pile with a formula showing on the top card, and a printed list of element symbols beside the pile.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the 20 formula cards. Shuffle them, with the formulas facing up. Put the symbol key where everyone can see it.

setup.art: A child holding up a card that reads CO₂ towards another player, keeping the back of the card turned towards herself.
setup.caption: 2. The reader holds up the top card. The next player says the atoms and how many.

setup.art: The reader turning the card over and reading the back aloud, while the other player counts on her fingers.
setup.caption: 3. The reader checks the back. Score 1 point for the atoms and 1 point for the name.

printables.title: 20 formula cards: a formula on the front, and its name and atoms on the back

items.b: Water. 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom. 3 atoms in each molecule.
Carbon dioxide. 1 carbon atom and 2 oxygen atoms. You breathe it out.
Sodium chloride, which is table salt. 1 sodium for every 1 chlorine.
Oxygen gas. 2 oxygen atoms. About one fifth of the air.
Nitrogen gas. 2 nitrogen atoms. About four fifths of the air.
Hydrogen gas. 2 hydrogen atoms. The lightest gas of all.
Carbon monoxide. 1 carbon atom and 1 oxygen atom. A poisonous gas.
Hydrogen peroxide. 2 hydrogen atoms and 2 oxygen atoms. It bleaches hair.
Ozone. 3 oxygen atoms. It blocks harmful rays high above the Earth.
Methane. 1 carbon atom and 4 hydrogen atoms. The main gas in CNG.
Ammonia. 1 nitrogen atom and 3 hydrogen atoms. A gas with a sharp smell.
Glucose. 6 carbon, 12 hydrogen and 6 oxygen atoms. The sugar in your blood.
Table sugar. 12 carbon, 22 hydrogen and 11 oxygen atoms. 45 atoms in each molecule.
Sodium hydrogen carbonate, which is baking soda. 1 sodium, 1 hydrogen and 1 carbon for every 3 oxygen.
Sodium carbonate, which is washing soda. 2 sodium and 1 carbon for every 3 oxygen.
Calcium carbonate. 1 calcium and 1 carbon for every 3 oxygen. Chalk, marble and eggshell.
Silicon dioxide, which is quartz. 1 silicon for every 2 oxygen. Most sand is quartz.
Propane. 3 carbon atoms and 8 hydrogen atoms. One of the gases in an LPG cylinder.
Potassium chloride. 1 potassium for every 1 chlorine. It is in ORS packets.
Gold. Only gold atoms, packed together. A metal is written with its symbol alone.

printables.title: 42 element symbols: the symbol key. Print one copy

rules: Shuffle the 20 cards and put them in a pile with the formulas facing up. Keep the symbol key where everyone can see it.
One player is the reader. The reader holds up the top card so that the next player sees only the formula.
That player says which atoms the formula has and how many. A right answer scores 1 point.
The same player then names the substance. A right name scores 1 more point. The reader checks both on the back.
If the player gets the atoms wrong, the player after them may try for 1 point.
The player who answered becomes the next reader. With two players, simply take turns.
Playing alone? Say the atoms and the name aloud, then turn the card over. Your score out of 40 is your result.
After all 20 cards, the player with the most points wins.

flow.do: Cut out the 20 formula cards and print the symbol key. Shuffle the cards with the formulas facing up.
flow.say: Each card has a formula on the front. The back gives its name and its atoms. The key shows what each symbol stands for.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Shuffle them, formulas up. Keep the key beside you.
flow.context: This is the first step of Read It Out. You set up the formula cards and the symbol key.

flow.do: Play the first ten cards. The answering player may look at the symbol key, but never at the back of a card.
flow.say: Look at the formula. Read it one symbol at a time. Say which atoms it has and how many. Then try to name the substance.
flow.kid: Read the formula one symbol at a time. Say the atoms. Then name it.

ask.q: This symbol has no small number after it. How many atoms of that kind are there?
good: One.
No number means one atom.

flow.parent: A common slip is to read Cl as the two symbols C and l. Another is to read CO as the metal cobalt, Co. Point to the capital letters. Every capital letter starts a new symbol.
flow.context: In this step of Read It Out you play the first ten formula cards.

flow.do: Play the last ten cards the same way. Keep the score on a piece of paper.
flow.say: Ten more cards. Some formulas are long. Take them one symbol at a time, as before.
flow.kid: Play ten more cards. Long formulas are read the same way.
flow.context: In this step of Read It Out you play the last ten formula cards and keep the score.

flow.do: Count the points. Then ask your child to find pairs of cards that differ by one atom. Lay each pair side by side.
flow.say: Find two cards that have the same elements but different numbers. Are they the same substance?
flow.kid: Find cards with the same elements but different numbers. Lay them together.

check.q: The cards CO and CO₂ have the same two elements. Are they the same substance?
options: No. CO₂ has one more oxygen atom.
Yes. The elements are the same.
check.why: Carbon monoxide, CO, is a poison. Carbon dioxide, CO₂, is the gas you breathe out. If you chose yes, look at the cards H₂O and H₂O₂ as well. One atom more makes a different substance.

flow.parent: The pairs are CO and CO₂, H₂O and H₂O₂, and O₂ and O₃. NaHCO₃ and Na₂CO₃ are also close.
flow.context: This is the last step of Read It Out. You find formula cards that differ by one atom, such as CO and CO₂.

games.title: Atom Market: collect atoms and build formulas
games.context: This is a card game about building formulas. You collect atom cards. Then you lay down the right atoms, in the right numbers, for the substances on a recipe sheet.

setup.art: A pile of small cards, each showing one large letter such as H, O or C, and a recipe sheet listing ten formulas in the middle of a table.
setup.caption: 1. Shuffle the 48 atom cards. Deal 5 to each player. Put the rest face down as the market pile.

setup.art: A child drawing two cards from the pile and adding them to the cards in her hand.
setup.caption: 2. On your turn, take 2 cards from the market pile.

setup.art: A child laying down three cards reading H, H and O in a row, and pointing to the line H₂O on the recipe sheet.
setup.caption: 3. Lay down the atoms of one formula. Say its name, its atoms and how many. Score its points.

printables.title: 48 atom cards: 16 hydrogen, 14 oxygen, 8 carbon, 4 nitrogen, 3 sodium and 3 chlorine
10 recipes: the recipe sheet. Print one copy
items: H₂: hydrogen gas. 2 hydrogen atoms. 2 points.
O₂: oxygen gas. 2 oxygen atoms. 2 points.
N₂: nitrogen gas. 2 nitrogen atoms. 2 points.
CO: carbon monoxide. 1 carbon atom and 1 oxygen atom. 2 points.
NaCl: sodium chloride, which is table salt. 1 sodium atom and 1 chlorine atom. 2 points.
H₂O: water. 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom. 3 points.
CO₂: carbon dioxide. 1 carbon atom and 2 oxygen atoms. 3 points.
H₂O₂: hydrogen peroxide. 2 hydrogen atoms and 2 oxygen atoms. 4 points.
NH₃: ammonia. 1 nitrogen atom and 3 hydrogen atoms. 4 points.
CH₄: methane. 1 carbon atom and 4 hydrogen atoms. 5 points.

rules: Shuffle the 48 atom cards. Deal 5 cards to each player. Put the rest face down in the middle as the market pile.
On your turn, first take 2 cards from the market pile.
Then you may lay down the atoms for one formula on the recipe sheet. You need exactly the right atoms in the right numbers.
As you lay the cards down, say the name, the atoms and how many. For example: water, two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
Score 1 point for each atom in the formula. Water scores 3 points and methane scores 5.
You may build each formula only once in a game. Cards you have laid down stay on the table.
If you cannot build anything, keep your cards and wait for your next turn.
When the market pile is empty, every player has one last turn. The player with the most points wins.
Playing alone? Deal yourself 5 cards and play the same way. Count how many turns you need to reach 15 points.

flow.do: Cut out the 48 atom cards and print the recipe sheet. Shuffle the cards and deal 5 to each player.
flow.say: Each card is one atom. The recipe sheet lists ten substances. To build one, you need exactly the atoms its formula asks for.
flow.kid: Cut out the atom cards. Deal five each. Put the recipe sheet in the middle.
flow.context: This is the first step of Atom Market. You deal the atom cards and lay out the recipe sheet.

flow.do: Play the first few rounds. Each player takes 2 cards, and then builds one formula if they can.
flow.say: Take two cards. Look at the recipe sheet. Do you hold the atoms for any formula? Lay them down and say what you have built.
flow.kid: Take two cards. Can you build a formula? Lay it down and name it.

ask.q: You hold one C and one O. What can you build now, and what could you build with one more O?
good: Carbon monoxide now.
Carbon dioxide with one more O.
CO scores 2 and CO₂ scores 3.

flow.parent: Let your child decide whether to build a small formula now or wait for a bigger one. Both choices are fair. Check that each player says the atoms and how many aloud.
flow.context: In this step of Atom Market you play the first rounds, taking two atom cards on each turn.

flow.do: Play on until the market pile is empty. Then every player has one last turn.
flow.say: The pile is getting small. Which formulas have you not built yet? Which atoms do you still need for them?
flow.kid: Play until the pile is empty. Then take one last turn each.
flow.context: In this step of Atom Market you play until the market pile of atom cards runs out.

flow.do: Count the points. Then look together at the cards that were never used.
flow.say: Look at the cards left in your hand. Why could you not use them? What would you have needed?
flow.kid: Count your points. Look at your unused cards. What did they need?

check.q: You hold 2 H cards and 2 O cards. Which formula on the recipe sheet uses all four?
check.why: H₂O₂ needs 2 hydrogen atoms and 2 oxygen atoms. Water needs only one O, so one card would be left over. Two water molecules would need 4 hydrogen atoms.

flow.parent: A leftover Na with no Cl, or a lone N, shows the main idea. A formula needs exact numbers, and nearly right does not count.
flow.context: This is the last step of Atom Market. You count the points and look at the atom cards nobody could use.

experiments.title: Count the Drops: does twice the lemon juice use up twice the iodine?
experiments.question: Lemon juice takes the colour out of iodine solution. How many drops of iodine can 1 teaspoon of lemon juice clear? How many can 2 teaspoons and 3 teaspoons clear?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Suppose 1 teaspoon of lemon juice clears some number of drops. Will 2 teaspoons clear the same number, a few more, or twice as many? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Squeeze all the lemons into one cup and strain the juice, so that every spoonful is the same juice. Use the same teaspoon, filled level. Put the same water, 2 tablespoons, and the same flour, a quarter of a teaspoon, in every glass. Take every drop from the same bottle. Stir after every drop. Stop at the same signal each time: the colour stays for a slow count of ten. Only the amount of lemon juice changes.
results_table: Drops of iodine before the colour stayed

materials.item: fresh lemons (nimbu), enough for 7 teaspoons of strained juice
iodine solution for cuts, the brown liquid sold as povidone-iodine at any medical shop
clear glasses or white cups
maida, rice flour or cornflour, 1 teaspoon in all
a teaspoon, a tablespoon and a tea strainer
drinking water, about half a tumbler
old newspaper to cover the table, and slips of paper for labels

experiments.safety: Iodine solution is for skin only. Nobody tastes it, or the liquids in the glasses. Pour everything down the sink at the end and rinse the glasses. Iodine stains cloth and wood yellow-brown, so cover the table and wear old clothes. Do not use it if your child is allergic to iodine.
experiments.record: Draw a table with four rows, for 0, 1, 2 and 3 teaspoons of lemon juice. Beside each, write the number of drops before the colour stayed.
experiments.context: In this experiment you add iodine, drop by drop, to glasses holding 1, 2 and 3 teaspoons of lemon juice. You count the drops each glass can clear before the colour stays.

setup.art: A clear glass of cloudy white water turning blue-grey where one brown drop has just fallen in.
setup.caption: 1. Stir a quarter teaspoon of flour into 2 tablespoons of water. Add 1 drop of iodine. This glass has no lemon juice. See the colour.

setup.art: Three clear glasses in a row labelled 1, 2 and 3, each holding cloudy water, with a teaspoon and a cup of strained lemon juice beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Make three more glasses of floury water. Add 1, 2 and 3 level teaspoons of lemon juice.

setup.art: A child stirring a glass with a spoon while a grown-up holds a small brown bottle above it and one drop falls.
setup.caption: 3. Add iodine one drop at a time. Stir after every drop and count.

setup.art: A glass that has stayed blue-grey, beside a notebook table with four rows of numbers.
setup.caption: 4. Stop when the colour stays for a slow count of ten. Write down the number of drops.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
cols: Drops of iodine before the colour stayed

flow.do: Cover the table with newspaper. Stir a quarter teaspoon of flour into 2 tablespoons of water in a glass. Add 1 drop of iodine and stir. Then squeeze in a few drops of lemon juice and stir again.
flow.say: Watch the glass while I add one drop of iodine. What colour is the water now? Now I will add a little lemon juice. What happened to the colour?
flow.kid: Add one drop of iodine to floury water. Stir it. Now add lemon juice. What happens?

ask.q: What do you think the lemon juice did to the iodine?
good: It took the colour away.
It changed the iodine into something with no colour.
It used the iodine up.

flow.parent: Iodine stains the starch in flour. The colour may be blue-grey, purple-grey or pale brown, depending on your flour and your bottle. Whatever colour you see is your signal. Lemon juice clears it within a few seconds of stirring. Do not explain yet.
flow.context: This is the first step of Count the Drops. You watch lemon juice take the colour out of a drop of iodine.

flow.do: Squeeze the lemons into one cup and strain the juice. Rinse the first glass. Make four glasses of floury water, as before, and label them 0, 1, 2 and 3. Add no juice to glass 0. Add 1, 2 and 3 level teaspoons of juice to the others. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: We will count how many drops each glass can clear. Suppose glass 1 clears some number of drops. Will glass 2 clear the same number, a few more, or twice as many? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: The glasses hold 1, 2 and 3 spoons of juice. Guess the drops for each. Say why.

ask.q: Why do we make one glass with no lemon juice at all?
good: To see how many drops colour plain floury water.
So we can compare the others with it.
To check that the lemon juice is what clears the iodine.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: In this step of Count the Drops you set up four glasses of lemon juice and guess the drop counts.

flow.do: Add iodine to glass 0, one drop at a time, and stir. It should colour with 1 or 2 drops. Then do glass 1 the same way. Your child stirs after every drop and counts aloud. Stop when the colour stays for a slow count of ten. Write both numbers.
flow.say: One drop. Stir. Has the colour gone? Then one more drop. We stop when the colour stays while you count slowly to ten.
flow.kid: Add one drop and stir. Count every drop. Stop when the colour stays.

check.q: In Count the Drops, why do you stir after every drop?
options: So the iodine meets all the lemon juice
check.why: The iodine loses its colour only where it meets lemon juice. Stirring brings them together. If you chose another answer, try one drop without stirring. A coloured patch stays where the drop fell.

flow.parent: Near the end the colour fades more slowly, so wait for the full count of ten. If glass 1 clears fewer than 4 drops, double the lemon juice in every glass. If it is still clearing after 30 drops, start again with half as much juice in every glass.
flow.context: In this step of Count the Drops you count the drops of iodine that 1 teaspoon of lemon juice clears.

flow.do: Do glass 2 and then glass 3 in the same way. Before each glass, ask your child to say how many drops they now expect. Write every count.
flow.say: Glass 1 took this many drops. How many do you expect for glass 2 now? Let us count and see.
flow.kid: Now do glass 2. Then do glass 3. Count the drops each time.
flow.context: In this step of Count the Drops you count the drops cleared by 2 and 3 teaspoons of lemon juice.

flow.do: Look at the four numbers together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they found, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at your four numbers. Say what you thought would happen, what you found, and why you think it happened. Could you have chosen how many drops glass 2 would clear?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you found. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Glass 2 held twice as much lemon juice as glass 1. What happened to the number of drops?
good: It was about twice as many.
It nearly doubled.
Three teaspoons took about three times as many.

ask.q: Why do you think the numbers go up in equal steps?
good: Each bit of lemon juice can clear only so much iodine.
More juice has more of whatever clears the iodine.
They react in a fixed amount.

flow.parent: Usually 2 teaspoons clear about twice as many drops as 1 teaspoon. 3 teaspoons clear about three times as many. A count may be 1 or 2 drops out, because the end is hard to judge. Write down what you really found. The reason: lemon juice holds vitamin C. Its formula is C₆H₈O₆. Iodine comes as molecules of two atoms, I₂. One vitamin C molecule changes exactly one iodine molecule into something with no colour. It can do this only once. So twice as many vitamin C molecules clear twice as many iodine molecules. Substances always react in fixed counts like this. That is why a formula can carry fixed numbers.
flow.think: A lemon from another tree may clear more drops, or fewer. Would 2 teaspoons of its juice still clear twice as many drops as 1 teaspoon?
flow.context: This is the last step of Count the Drops. You say what your drop counts show about 1, 2 and 3 teaspoons of lemon juice.

experiments.title: Water from a Dry Powder: which white powder can give off water?
experiments.question: Salt and baking soda are both dry white powders. The formula of salt is NaCl. The formula of baking soda is NaHCO₃. If each is heated, will either of them give off water?
experiments.predict: Before the heating starts, guess. Water is H₂O. Look at the two formulas. Will salt give off water, will baking soda, will both, or will neither? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same dry pan, the same low flame and the same amount of powder, 2 level teaspoons. Cover the pan with the same steel plate, cooled under the tap and wiped dry each time. Keep the plate on for the same time, a slow count of twenty. Check at 1 minute, 3 minutes and 5 minutes. Look only at the middle of the plate, inside the ring where the pan touched it. Only the powder changes.

materials.item: table salt, 2 level teaspoons
baking soda (cooking soda), 2 level teaspoons. Do not use baking powder, which is a mixture
a small steel or aluminium pan, old and completely dry. Do not use a non-stick pan
a flat steel plate or lid that covers the pan fully
a dry steel spoon, a thick cloth or tongs, and a clock
two slips of paper with NaCl and NaHCO₃ written on them

experiments.safety: A grown-up does all the heating and handles the hot pan and plate. Keep the flame low. Salt may crackle and jump, so keep faces away from the pan. The powder left from the baking soda is washing soda, which stings eyes and skin. Do not taste or touch it. When it is cool, wash it down the sink with plenty of water.
experiments.record: Draw a table with two rows, for salt and baking soda. For each check, at 1, 3 and 5 minutes, write wet or dry. Also write what the powder looked like as it was heated.
experiments.context: In this experiment a grown-up heats salt and then baking soda in a dry pan. You cover the pan with a cold steel plate and see which powder wets the plate.

setup.art: Two small heaps of white powder on two saucers, each with a paper slip in front reading NaCl or NaHCO₃.
setup.caption: 1. Put 2 level teaspoons of salt and of baking soda on two saucers. Read their formulas.

setup.art: A grown-up heating a small dry steel pan of white powder on a low gas flame, with a child watching from a step back.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up heats the salt in a dry pan on a low flame.

setup.art: A flat steel plate sitting on top of the small pan like a lid, and a clock beside the stove.
setup.caption: 3. At 1, 3 and 5 minutes, cover the pan with a cold, dry plate for a slow count of twenty.

setup.art: A grown-up holding the plate turned over with a cloth, while a child looks at tiny drops of water in the middle of it.
setup.caption: 4. Lift the plate and turn it over. Is the middle wet or dry? Then do the same with the baking soda.

flow.do: Put the two powders on saucers, with the formula slips in front. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: Both powders are dry. Water is H₂O. Look at the two formulas. Could either powder give off water when I heat it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Read the two formulas. Water is H₂O. Which powder could give off water? Why?

ask.q: Which atoms would a powder need in order to make water?
good: Hydrogen and oxygen.
It needs H and O.
Salt has neither of them.

flow.parent: Many children say that neither will, because both powders are dry. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of Water from a Dry Powder. You read the formulas NaCl and NaHCO₃ and guess which powder can give off water.

flow.do: Heat 2 level teaspoons of salt in the dry pan on a low flame. Stir now and then with the dry spoon. At 1, 3 and 5 minutes, cover the pan with the cold, dry plate for a slow count of twenty. Lift the plate with the cloth and turn it over.
flow.say: I will heat the salt. You watch the clock and tell me when each minute comes. Each time, look at the middle of the plate. Is it wet or dry?
flow.kid: A grown-up heats the salt. Look at the plate each time. Is it wet or dry?
flow.parent: Cool the plate under the tap and wipe it dry before every check. Salt that has been open in damp weather may mist the plate faintly at the first check. After that it stays dry. Drops near the rim come from the gas flame, so look only at the middle.
flow.context: In this step of Water from a Dry Powder a grown-up heats salt. You check a cold plate each time.

flow.do: Switch off the flame. Tip the hot salt onto a steel plate to cool. Wipe the pan with a dry cloth.
flow.say: The salt is done. I will empty the pan and wipe it. The pan must be dry before the next powder goes in. Why?
flow.kid: A grown-up empties the pan and wipes it dry. Why must it be dry?
flow.context: In this step of Water from a Dry Powder a grown-up empties the salt from the pan and dries it.

flow.do: Heat 2 level teaspoons of baking soda in the same way. Stir gently. Watch the powder itself as well. Check with the cold, dry plate at 1, 3 and 5 minutes.
flow.say: Now the baking soda. Watch the powder as well as the plate. What is the powder doing? Now look at the middle of the plate.
flow.kid: A grown-up heats the baking soda. Watch the powder move. Check the plate each time.

check.q: In Water from a Dry Powder, why is the plate cooled and dried before every check?
options: So old drops are not counted again
check.why: A wet plate would look wet whatever the powder did. A warm plate would let the water escape as gas. If you chose another answer, remember that a fair test starts the same way every time.

flow.parent: After a minute or two the powder seems to shiver, and small puffs lift it. That is gas leaving. The plate should come away with a mist or clear drops in the middle. By 5 minutes there is usually less.
flow.context: In this step of Water from a Dry Powder a grown-up heats baking soda. You check a cold plate each time.

flow.do: Switch off the flame and leave the pan to cool. Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at your table. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. Where could the water have come from?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: The baking soda was dry. Where did the water come from?
good: From the hydrogen and oxygen atoms in the baking soda.
The heat rearranged the atoms into water.
Its formula has H and O in it.

ask.q: Could any amount of heating get water out of the salt?
good: No. Salt has no hydrogen or oxygen atoms.
No. Its formula is only Na and Cl.

flow.parent: The reason: baking soda is NaHCO₃. Heat rearranges its atoms into three new substances. They are water, carbon dioxide gas and washing soda, Na₂CO₃. The water leaves as steam and turns back to drops on the cold plate. The carbon dioxide is what lifts the powder in puffs. Salt is NaCl. It has no hydrogen and no oxygen, so it has nothing to build water from. If you own a kitchen scale, weigh the baking soda before and after. About 10 grams becomes about 6 grams, which is too big a loss to be dampness.
flow.think: Sugar is C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁. Does its formula hold the atoms that water needs?
flow.context: This is the last step of Water from a Dry Powder. You say why heated baking soda wet the plate and heated salt did not.

activities.title: The Name Collector: how many names does one substance have?

materials.item: a tumbler of water, and the jars or packets of salt, sugar and baking soda from your kitchen
a sheet of paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Collect every name your family knows for water, salt, sugar and baking soda. Then add the chemical name and the formula of each.

activities.record: Draw a table with four rows, for water, salt, sugar and baking soda. Make three columns: everyday names, chemical name and formula.
activities.context: In this activity you collect every name your family knows for water, salt, sugar and baking soda. Then you add the formula of each and see which column never changes.

setup.caption: 1. Put water, salt, sugar and baking soda on the table. Write every name your family knows for each.

setup.art: A child reading the small print on the back of a baking soda packet.
setup.caption: 2. Read the packets. Look for a name in small print that sounds like chemistry.
