setup.caption: 3. Add the chemical name and the formula of each. Which column would be the same in every country?

flow.do: Put the water, salt, sugar and baking soda on the table. Draw the table with four rows. Ask everyone at home for names in every language they know.
flow.say: What do we call this at home? What does your grandmother call it? What is it called in the other languages we know? Write every name.
flow.kid: Write every name you know for water, salt, sugar and baking soda.
flow.parent: Some examples for salt are uppu, namak and nun. For water there are thanneer, neeru, vellam, paani and jol. Baking soda is also called cooking soda, soda uppu, meetha soda and khabar soda.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Name Collector. You write every everyday name your family knows for four kitchen substances.

flow.do: Read the packets together. Then write these in the last two columns. Water: water, H₂O. Salt: sodium chloride, NaCl. Sugar: sucrose, C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁. Baking soda: sodium hydrogen carbonate, NaHCO₃.
flow.say: Look at the small print on the baking soda. Can you find a name there that we never use at home? Now copy the chemical names and the formulas.
flow.kid: Read the packets. Find a name you never use at home. Copy the formulas.
flow.parent: Packets often say sodium bicarbonate, which is an older chemical name for sodium hydrogen carbonate. Chemists call water simply water. Sucrose is the agreed short name for table sugar.
flow.context: In this step of the Name Collector you add each substance's chemical name and formula to your table.

flow.do: Look at the finished table. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Look at the three columns. Which column would a child in Japan or Brazil write differently from you? Which would she write exactly the same?
flow.kid: Which column changes from country to country? Which column never changes?

check.q: Which of these tells you what salt is made of?
check.why: NaCl says that salt has sodium and chlorine, one for one. Uppu and namak are good names, and millions of people use them. But a name like these does not say what the substance is made of.

flow.think: Is one of these names more real than the others?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Name Collector. You compare the everyday names with the formulas in your table.

activities.title: Dough Atoms: build H₂O, CO₂ and a grain of salt

materials.item: chapati dough, three lumps each as big as a lemon
turmeric powder, half a teaspoon, to colour one lump yellow
coffee powder, tea dust or cocoa, 1 teaspoon, to colour one lump brown
a plate, a sheet of paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Make dough atoms in three colours. Build models of water, carbon dioxide and other molecules, and a small block of salt.

activities.record: Draw each model you built and write its formula under it. For the salt block, write how many balls of each colour you used.
activities.context: In this activity you make atoms from three colours of chapati dough. You build molecules from formulas, write formulas from models, and build a small block of salt.

setup.art: Three lumps of dough on a plate, one plain, one yellow and one brown, with a paper key beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Colour one lump yellow with turmeric and one brown with coffee powder. Write a key: plain is hydrogen, yellow is oxygen, brown is carbon.

setup.art: A yellow dough ball with two small plain balls pressed onto it in a wide V, and a brown ball with a yellow ball pressed on each side.
setup.caption: 2. Build water, H₂O, and carbon dioxide, CO₂. Press the balls together.

setup.art: A grown-up hiding a dough model behind a book while a child writes on paper.
setup.caption: 3. One person builds a hidden model. The other writes its formula.

setup.art: A small cube made of eight dough balls, four yellow and four plain, with the colours alternating.
setup.caption: 4. Build a cube of salt from 4 yellow and 4 plain balls. Each ball's nearest neighbours must be the other colour.

flow.do: Knead turmeric into one lump of dough and coffee powder into another. Write the key on paper. Roll 8 small plain balls, each the size of a chana. Roll 6 yellow and 2 brown balls, each the size of a grape.
flow.say: These balls are our atoms. Plain is hydrogen, yellow is oxygen and brown is carbon. The colours are our own choice. The numbers will not be.
flow.kid: Make three colours of dough. Roll small plain balls and bigger yellow and brown ones.
flow.context: This is the first step of Dough Atoms. You make dough balls in three colours to stand for hydrogen, oxygen and carbon atoms.

flow.do: Write H₂, O₂, H₂O and CO₂ on the paper. Your child builds each one by pressing balls together, and says the atoms aloud.
flow.say: Read the first formula. Which atoms does it need, and how many? Build it. Now read it back to me from your model.
flow.kid: Read each formula. Build it from dough. Say the atoms aloud.

ask.q: In CO₂, which atom does the small 2 belong to?
good: The oxygen.
The O, because the 2 comes after it.
There is only one carbon.

flow.parent: In water the two hydrogen atoms sit on the oxygen in a wide V. In carbon dioxide the three atoms sit in a straight line, with the carbon in the middle.
flow.context: In this step of Dough Atoms you build hydrogen gas, oxygen gas, water and carbon dioxide from their formulas.

flow.do: Take turns. One person builds a model behind a book, and the other writes its formula. Use CO, O₃, CH₄ and H₂O₂. Break up old models when you need more balls.
flow.say: I have built something behind this book. Look at it now. Count each colour and write the formula.
flow.kid: Look at the hidden model. Count each colour. Write its formula.

check.q: A model has 1 brown carbon ball and 4 small hydrogen balls. What is its formula?
check.why: The small number comes after the symbol it counts. There is one carbon, so C has no number. There are four hydrogen atoms, so H is followed by a small 4. If you chose C₄H, read it back: it says four carbons and one hydrogen.

flow.parent: H₂O₂ is two yellow balls joined to each other, with one small plain ball on each. Ask how it differs from water.
flow.context: In this step of Dough Atoms you write the formula of a dough model that someone else has built.

flow.do: Roll 4 new yellow balls and 4 new plain balls, all the same size. For this model only, yellow stands for sodium and plain stands for chlorine. Build a cube, two balls along each edge. The balls beside, above and below each ball must be the other colour.
flow.say: Now we build salt. Yellow is sodium and plain is chlorine this time. Build a cube where the colours take turns. How many of each did you use? Can you find one piece that is a molecule of salt?
flow.kid: Build a cube of 8 balls. The colours must take turns. Count each colour.

ask.q: Pick one yellow ball. How many plain balls touch it? Which one is its partner?
good: Three plain balls touch it.
It has no single partner.
It belongs to all of them equally.

ask.q: So what does the formula NaCl tell you about the block?
good: There is one sodium for every chlorine.
The numbers are equal.
It is a ratio.

flow.parent: The block has 4 of each, so the ratio is one to one. In a real grain each sodium atom has six chlorine neighbours. Nothing in the block is a separate pair, which is why salt has no molecules.
flow.context: This is the last step of Dough Atoms. You build a small block of salt from 8 dough balls and count the two kinds.

activities.title: Clues Inside a Name: read a toothpaste tube and an ORS packet

materials.item: a toothpaste tube or its box
an ORS packet, or any medicine or food packet with a list of ingredients
the symbol key from the game Read It Out, or any periodic table
a sheet of paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Find the chemical names on two packets. Use the clues inside each name to say which elements are in the substance.

activities.record: Write each chemical name you find. Under it, write the elements you can spot in the name and their symbols.
activities.context: In this activity you read the ingredients on a toothpaste tube and an ORS packet. You find the element names inside the chemical names, and learn what ide, ate and di mean.

setup.art: A toothpaste box and an ORS packet turned to show their ingredient lists, with a pencil underlining one line.
setup.caption: 1. Find the list of ingredients on each packet. Underline every name that has sodium, potassium or calcium in it.

setup.art: A paper with the words sodium fluoride split by a pencil line into two parts, and the symbols Na and F written underneath.
setup.caption: 2. Split each name into its parts. Find each part in the symbol key.

setup.art: A child's tally chart with the words sodium, potassium and calcium and a row of tally marks beside each.
setup.caption: 3. Count how many times each element appears. Which one wins?

flow.do: Find the ingredients on both packets. Your child underlines every name that includes sodium, potassium or calcium, and copies each onto paper.
flow.say: These lists use chemical names. Hunt for the words sodium, potassium and calcium. Underline every name that has one of them.
flow.kid: Find the ingredient lists. Underline names with sodium, potassium or calcium.
flow.parent: Toothpaste often lists sodium fluoride or sodium monofluorophosphate, and calcium carbonate. ORS lists sodium chloride, potassium chloride and sodium citrate. Lists differ from brand to brand.
flow.context: This is the first step of Clues Inside a Name. You hunt for chemical names on a toothpaste tube and an ORS packet.

flow.do: Take three of the names. For each, ask which elements are in it. Explain the endings below only after your child has guessed.
flow.say: Look at sodium chloride. Which two elements can you hear in that name? What might the ending ide be telling us?
flow.kid: Split each name into parts. Which elements can you hear in it?

ask.q: Which elements are in potassium chloride?
good: Potassium and chlorine.
K and Cl.

flow.parent: A name ending in ide usually has just two elements. Sodium chloride is sodium and chlorine. A name ending in ate has oxygen in it as well. Calcium carbonate is calcium, carbon and oxygen. Di means two, as in titanium dioxide.
flow.context: In this step of Clues Inside a Name you split chemical names, such as sodium chloride, into their elements.

flow.do: Tally how many names include sodium, how many potassium and how many calcium. Then write formulas for the names with two elements, using the symbol key.
flow.say: Which element appears most often on our packets? Now try to write sodium chloride and potassium chloride in symbols.
flow.kid: Count each element. Which appears most? Write two of the names in symbols.

check.q: A tube lists sodium fluoride. Which two elements are in it?
check.why: The first word names the metal, sodium. The second word is the other element with its ending changed to ide, so fluoride comes from fluorine. Its formula is NaF. If you chose sulfur and iron, check the key: sulfur is S and iron is Fe.

flow.parent: Sodium usually wins. Sodium chloride is NaCl, potassium chloride is KCl and sodium fluoride is NaF.
flow.context: This is the last step of Clues Inside a Name. You count the elements you found and write two names as formulas.

activities.title: CHeNNaI: write names with element symbols

materials.item: the symbol key from the game Read It Out, or any periodic table
a sheet of paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Try to write the names of people and places using only element symbols.

activities.record: Write every name you managed, with capital and small letters exactly as in the symbols. Write one name that cannot be done, and which letter stopped you.
activities.context: In this activity you try to write names of people and places using only element symbols. It is practice in telling one-letter symbols from two-letter symbols.

setup.art: The word CHeNNaI written in large letters with a pencil line between each symbol: C, He, N, Na, I.
setup.caption: 1. Chennai can be written with five symbols: C, He, N, Na and I.

setup.art: A child with the symbol key beside her, trying to write her own name in symbols on paper.
setup.caption: 2. Try your own name and your town. Use only symbols from the key.

setup.art: A list of names in mixed capital and small letters, with one name crossed out and the letter J circled.
setup.caption: 3. Find a name that cannot be written, and the letter that stops you.

flow.do: Write CHeNNaI on the paper. Ask your child to split it into symbols, using the symbol key.
flow.say: This is Chennai, written only in element symbols. Where does each symbol begin? How can you tell?
flow.kid: Split CHeNNaI into element symbols. Every capital letter starts a new symbol.

ask.q: How do you know that He is one symbol and not two?
good: The e is small.
A small letter belongs to the capital before it.
Every capital starts a new symbol.

flow.parent: The answer is carbon, helium, nitrogen, sodium and iodine.
flow.context: This is the first step of CHeNNaI. You split the word into the five element symbols it is written with.

flow.do: Your child tries to write other names with symbols from the key. Start with KOCHI, PUNe, AgRa, SiTa, TaRa and MoNa. Then try names from your own family.
flow.say: Now try Kochi, Pune and Agra. Then try your own name. You may use only symbols that are in the key.
flow.kid: Write Kochi, Pune and Agra in symbols. Then try your own name.
flow.parent: KOCHI is K, O, C, H, I. PUNe is P, U, Ne. AgRa is Ag, Ra. Many names cannot be done, and finding out why is part of the fun.
flow.context: In this step of CHeNNaI you write the names of towns and people using only element symbols.

flow.do: Ask which names were impossible and which letter stopped them.
flow.say: Which names could you not write? Which letter stopped you each time?
flow.kid: Which name was impossible? Which letter stopped you?

check.q: What is the difference between Co and CO?
options: Co is one element. CO is two.
CO is a louder way to write Co.
check.why: Co is cobalt, a metal. CO is one carbon atom and one oxygen atom, which is the gas carbon monoxide. If you chose another answer, remember that every capital letter starts a new symbol.

flow.parent: No element symbol contains J or Q, so Jaya and Qasim cannot be written. With this key there is also no way to write a D.
flow.context: This is the last step of CHeNNaI. You find which letters no element symbol can supply.

projects.title: The Formula Trail: hide eight formulas around your home

materials.item: small cards or slips of thick paper
a pencil or sketch pen, and sticky tape
the 20 formula cards from the game Read It Out, to copy from

schedule.what: Choose eight substances in your home. Write a formula card for each and tape it beside the substance.
Lead someone along the trail. They read each formula aloud as atoms and name the substance. Record which cards were hardest.

projects.record: A table with eight rows and four columns: the formula, the substance, where the card is taped, and whether your reader named it at the first try.
projects.context: In this two-day project you tape eight formula cards beside the real substances in your home. On the second day someone follows the trail and reads every formula.

setup.art: A child writing H₂O on a small card at a table, with a list of eight substances beside her.
setup.caption: 1. Choose eight substances at home. Write the formula of each on a card.

setup.art: A small card reading NaCl taped to a kitchen shelf beside a salt jar.
setup.caption: 2. Tape each card beside its substance, with the formula showing and the name on the back.

setup.art: A grown-up reading a card taped beside a kitchen tap, while a child with a notebook watches.
setup.caption: 3. Next day, lead someone along the trail. They read each formula as atoms and name the substance.

flow.do: Day 1. Walk round the home together and choose eight substances. Your child writes each formula on a card, with the name on the back.
flow.say: Which eight substances shall we label? Find the formula of each on the cards from Read It Out. Write the name on the back.
flow.kid: Choose eight substances at home. Write a formula card for each.
flow.parent: Easy ones are water at the tap (H₂O), salt (NaCl), sugar (C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁), baking soda (NaHCO₃) and an egg's shell (CaCO₃). A soda bottle can carry CO₂, a gold ornament Au and an open window O₂.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Formula Trail. You choose eight substances at home and write a formula card for each.

flow.do: Day 1. Your child tapes each card beside its substance, at the height of their own eyes. Then they draw the table with eight rows.
flow.say: Tape each card where a reader will find it. Keep the formula facing out. Now draw your table for tomorrow.
flow.kid: Tape each card beside its substance. Draw a table with eight rows.
flow.wait: Leave the cards up until the next day.
flow.context: In this step of the Formula Trail you tape your eight formula cards around the home and draw the table.

flow.do: Day 2. Your child leads a reader along the trail. At each card the reader says the atoms and how many, and then names the substance. Your child records yes or no.
flow.say: You are the guide today. At each card, ask your reader which atoms it shows and how many. Then ask what the substance is.
flow.kid: Lead a reader along your trail. Ask for the atoms and the name each time.

ask.q: Which card was hardest for your reader? Why do you think so?
good: The long one for sugar.
The one with a two-letter symbol.
They did not know what Na stands for.

flow.parent: The reader can be a parent, a sibling, a neighbour or a grandparent on a video call. If nobody is free, be the reader yourself and let your child check you.
flow.context: This is day 2 of the Formula Trail. Someone follows your eight cards and reads each formula aloud.

flow.do: Day 2. Look at the table together and talk about the question below.
flow.say: Your reader knew every one of these substances by name already. What did the formula tell them that the name did not?
flow.kid: What did each formula tell your reader that the name did not?
flow.think: Would a visitor who speaks only Japanese be able to follow your trail?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Formula Trail. You look at which formula cards your reader found hard.

challenges.title: A Better Code? Invent your own way to write substances
challenges.problem: Before 1813 chemists had no shared way to write a substance. John Dalton drew circles with marks inside. Jöns Jacob Berzelius used letters and numbers. Your problem is the one they faced. Invent a code for five elements: hydrogen, oxygen, carbon, sodium and chlorine. With it, write water, carbon dioxide, table salt, methane and hydrogen peroxide.
constraints: The code must show which atoms are in the substance and how many of each.
Each of the five substances must take less than 10 seconds to write.
A person who has your key must be able to read all five without asking you anything.
Water and hydrogen peroxide must look different, and so must any other two substances.
You may not use the real symbols H, O, C, Na and Cl.
materials: sheets of paper and a pencil
sketch pens or crayons, if you want to use colour
a clock or a phone that shows seconds
a second person to test your code
general: Draw a small picture for each element, such as a drop for hydrogen and a flame for oxygen. Repeat the picture once for each atom.
Use a different shape for each element, as Dalton did, and draw one shape for each atom.
Use a colour for each element and write a number in that colour.
creative: Use dots, as on a dice face, to show how many atoms there are. The reader can then see the number without counting.
Use sounds as well as marks. Give each element a short syllable, so that the code can be spoken over a phone.
Arrange the marks to show which atom is in the middle, which a real formula does not show.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own code and test it. Write the five substances while someone times you. Then hand your key and your five codes to a reader. Record how many they read correctly. Last, write one thing your code does better than letters and one thing it does worse.
challenges.context: In this challenge you invent your own code for writing substances and test it on another person. It is the problem chemists solved when they agreed on letters and small numbers.

setup.art: A child's page showing an invented key: a small shape drawn beside each of the words hydrogen, oxygen, carbon, sodium and chlorine.
setup.caption: 1. Invent a mark for each of the five elements. Write your key.

setup.art: The same child writing five short codes while a grown-up watches a clock.
setup.caption: 2. Write the five substances in your code. Each must take less than 10 seconds.

setup.art: A second person reading the codes with the key beside them and writing down the substances.
setup.caption: 3. Give your key and your codes to a reader. How many can they read?

flow.do: Read the problem together. Your child tries the first idea that comes to mind and writes water with it.
flow.say: Chemists once had no shared code. You will make one. Start with any idea and write water with it. What must your code show?
flow.kid: Invent a mark for each element. Write water with your marks.

ask.q: What two things must any code for a substance show?
good: Which atoms are in it.
How many of each atom there are.

flow.context: This is the first step of A Better Code. You try a first idea for writing water without the letters H and O.

flow.do: Your child finishes the key and writes all five substances. Time each one. Any that takes 10 seconds or more must be made simpler.
flow.say: Write all five. I will time you. If one takes too long, how could you make the mark simpler?
flow.kid: Write all five substances in your code. Each must take under 10 seconds.
flow.parent: The five are water (2 hydrogen, 1 oxygen), carbon dioxide (1 carbon, 2 oxygen), table salt (1 sodium, 1 chlorine), methane (1 carbon, 4 hydrogen) and hydrogen peroxide (2 hydrogen, 2 oxygen).
flow.context: In this step of A Better Code you write five substances in your own code and time yourself.

flow.do: Give the key and the five codes to a second person. They write what each code says, without help. Count how many are right.
flow.say: Hand over your key and your codes. Say nothing while your reader works. Which code did they read wrongly, and why?
flow.kid: Give your key and codes to a reader. Stay quiet. Count the right answers.

check.q: A reader mixes up your codes for water and hydrogen peroxide. What should you change?
options: Make the number of atoms clearer
check.why: Water and hydrogen peroxide have the same elements. Only the number of oxygen atoms differs. So the code must make the numbers easy to see. Colour and size do not fix that.

flow.context: In this step of A Better Code another person reads your five codes using only your key.

flow.do: Compare the code with H₂O, CO₂ and NaCl. Your child writes one thing their code does better and one thing it does worse.
flow.say: Now write the same five in real formulas. Which is faster? Which could be typed on any phone? What does your code show that letters do not?
flow.kid: Compare your code with real formulas. What is better? What is worse?
flow.parent: Praise an honest list of faults as much as a clever code. Letters won because anyone can write, print and say them. Pictures can show the arrangement of atoms, and chemists use drawings for that.
flow.context: This is the last step of A Better Code. You compare your own code with the letters and numbers that chemists use.

items.p: What does the small 2 in H₂O tell you?
opts: Each molecule has two hydrogen atoms
Each molecule has two oxygen atoms
There are two molecules of water
Water is twice as heavy as air
items.why: A small number counts the atoms of the symbol just before it. The 2 comes after the H, so it counts hydrogen atoms.

items.p: The formula of table salt is ____.
items.why: Na is the symbol for sodium and Cl is the symbol for chlorine. Table salt is sodium chloride.

items.p: Match each symbol to its element.
items.why: H, O and C are the first letters of the English names. Na comes from natrium, the old Latin name of sodium. Cl is the first two letters of chlorine.

items.p: In a formula, a symbol with no small number after it means one atom.
items.why: True. In H₂O the O has no number, so there is one oxygen atom.

items.p: How many atoms are there in one molecule of CO₂?
items.why: One carbon atom and two oxygen atoms make three atoms.

items.p: Which of these is the formula of carbon dioxide?
items.why: Di means two. Carbon dioxide has one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms. CO is carbon monoxide, and Co is the metal cobalt.

items.p: Sort these formulas. Does each have one kind of atom, or more than one kind?
items.why: Count the different symbols. O₂, Au and N₂ each have one symbol, so they are elements. The others have two symbols, so they are compounds.

items.p: The symbol for sodium is So.
items.why: False. The symbol is Na, from natrium, the old Latin name of sodium.

items.p: In water there are ____ hydrogen atoms for every one oxygen atom.
items.why: The formula H₂O has a small 2 after the H and no number after the O.

items.p: What does the formula NaCl tell you about salt?
items.why: Na is sodium and Cl is chlorine, with no numbers, so they are one to one. Cl is one symbol. It is not carbon followed by another element.

items.p: Write what the formula CO₂ tells you, in one full sentence.
items.a: Each molecule of carbon dioxide has one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms.
items.why: A strong answer names both elements and gives the number of each.

items.p: In Count the Drops, twice the lemon juice cleared about twice the iodine. Explain why.
items.a: Lemon juice holds vitamin C. One vitamin C molecule changes exactly one iodine molecule. So twice as many vitamin C molecules clear twice as many iodine molecules.
items.why: A strong answer says that the two substances react in a fixed count, one for one. So the amounts go up together.

items.p: Draw one molecule of water and one molecule of carbon dioxide as circles. Label every atom.
items.a: Water: one circle marked O with two smaller circles marked H joined to it. Carbon dioxide: one circle marked C with a circle marked O joined on each side.
items.why: A strong drawing has the right number of each atom, and every circle is labelled with its symbol.
items.art: A blank box with the formulas H₂O and CO₂ written above it.

items.p: Which is the real name of water?

views.says: It is thanneer. My family has called it that for hundreds of years, and everyone here understands it.
It is H₂O. That name says what water is made of, and it is the same in every country.
No name is the real one. Water was here long before there was any word for it.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. One reason is that a name is useful when the people you talk to understand it. Another is that only the formula says what water is made of. Another is that water does not change when its name changes.
items.why: Each view has something right in it. A strong answer says what a name is for, and uses that to choose.

items.p: Why is the second letter of a symbol always small?
opts: So Co and CO cannot be confused
Because small letters are quicker to write
Because the second atom is smaller
items.why: Every capital letter starts a new symbol. Co is one element, cobalt. CO is two elements, carbon and oxygen.

worksheets.title: One atom more, and names that give clues

items.p: Carbon monoxide is CO. Carbon dioxide is CO₂. What is the difference between their molecules?
opts: CO₂ has one more oxygen atom
CO₂ has one more carbon atom
CO₂ is two molecules of CO
items.why: The small 2 counts oxygen atoms. That one extra atom makes a different gas. Carbon monoxide is a deadly poison.

items.p: Which pair shows two different substances made of the same two elements?
items.why: Water and hydrogen peroxide are both made of hydrogen and oxygen. The numbers differ, so the substances differ.

items.p: Salt has no separate molecules. So what does its formula NaCl mean?
opts: Equal numbers of sodium and chlorine
One sodium atom in each grain
One molecule made of two atoms
items.why: Salt is a crystal in which sodium and chlorine atoms alternate. The formula gives the ratio, which is one to one.

items.p: What does 'di' mean in the name carbon dioxide?
items.why: Di means two. Carbon dioxide has two oxygen atoms. Mono means one, as in carbon monoxide.

items.p: Glucose and fructose have the same formula, so they are the same substance.
items.why: False. Both are C₆H₁₂O₆, but their atoms are arranged differently. They are two different sugars, called isomers.

items.p: Water from a cloud and water from a well have the same formula.
items.why: True. Pure water is H₂O wherever it comes from. Well water also has other substances dissolved in it.

items.p: Sort these. Was each one chosen by people, or found by measuring?
items: Equal sodium and chlorine in salt
items.why: Letters, words and symbols are agreements, and they could have been different. The numbers of atoms had to be measured, and nobody could choose them.

items.p: Three of these substances contain oxygen atoms. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Water, carbon dioxide and ozone all have O in their formulas. Salt has only sodium and chlorine.

items.p: How many atoms are there in one molecule of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆?
items.why: 6 carbon, 12 hydrogen and 6 oxygen atoms. 6 + 12 + 6 = 24.

items.p: Put these molecules in order, from the fewest atoms to the most.
items.why: O₂ has 2 atoms, H₂O has 3, CH₄ has 5 and C₆H₁₂O₆ has 24.

items.p: In Water from a Dry Powder, only the heated baking soda wet the plate. Explain why, using NaHCO₃ and NaCl.
items.a: Water is H₂O, so it needs hydrogen and oxygen atoms. Baking soda has both, and heat rearranged them into water. Salt has neither, so it cannot make water.
items.why: A strong answer says that heating only rearranges atoms. A substance can give off only what its own atoms can build.

items.p: A packet says 'chemical-free'. Can anything be chemical-free? Explain what you think.
items.a: No. Everything made of atoms is a chemical. Water is H₂O and salt is NaCl. The packet probably means that nothing harmful was added.
items.why: A strong answer says that natural things have formulas too. Whether a substance harms you depends on which substance it is and how much.

items.p: How could you find out whether water has one or two hydrogen atoms for each oxygen atom?
items.a: Split water with electricity and collect the two gases. The hydrogen takes up twice as much space as the oxygen. That points to two hydrogen atoms for each oxygen atom.
items.why: A strong answer names a measurement. The number in a formula has to be found by measuring.

items.p: Should every country use the same chemical symbols?

views.says: Symbols should come from our own languages. Na means nothing in Tamil, so I have to learn it by heart.
One shared set is worth the effort. A label written in Japan can be read in India, and no medicine is mixed up.
Shared symbols are useful. But they come from Latin and from European names, and most of the world was never asked.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. A strong answer weighs what everyone gains from one shared code. It also says what is hard or unfair about how the code was chosen.
items.why: This is a real trade-off. Shared symbols save lives and time. They also carry the history of the people who chose them.

items.p: Label the three parts of the formula H₂O in this picture.
a: Small 2: there are two hydrogen atoms
O: the symbol for oxygen, with no number, so one atom
items.why: A formula is read one symbol at a time. A small number belongs to the symbol just before it.
items.art: The formula H₂O written very large, with three blank label lines pointing to the H, the small 2 and the O.

worksheets.title: What a formula can and cannot tell you

items.p: A white powder has the formula KCl. Heated alone, could it give off water?
opts: No. It has no hydrogen or oxygen.
Yes. Every powder holds some water.
Yes, if it is heated long enough.
Only if the powder is white.
items.why: Water is H₂O. Heating only rearranges the atoms a substance already has. KCl has potassium and chlorine atoms only.

items.p: Which part of a formula did people have to measure to find?
items.why: The letters were agreed by people. The numbers of atoms had to be found by measuring, as with the gases from split water.

items.p: 3 teaspoons of lemon juice cleared 24 drops of iodine. About how many drops would 1 teaspoon clear?
items.why: The same juice clears drops in a fixed proportion. One third of the juice clears one third of the drops. 24 ÷ 3 = 8.

items.p: Vitamin B12 has the formula C₆₃H₈₈CoN₁₄O₁₄P. What does Co stand for?
items.why: A capital letter followed by a small letter is one symbol. Co is cobalt. Carbon and oxygen would be written CO.

items.p: Heating a substance alone can add new kinds of atoms to it.
items.why: False. Heating rearranges the atoms that are already there. It cannot make a new kind of atom.

items.p: Two substances with different formulas can look exactly alike.
items.why: True. Salt, NaCl, and baking soda, NaHCO₃, are both dry white powders. You need a test or a label to tell them apart.

items.p: Match each everyday name to its chemical name.
items.why: An everyday name says how people use a substance. A chemical name says which elements are in it.

items.p: How many oxygen atoms are there in 4 molecules of CO₂?
items.why: Each molecule has 2 oxygen atoms. 4 × 2 = 8.

items.p: Different substances that have the same formula are called ____.
items.why: Isomers have the same atoms in the same numbers, joined in a different arrangement. Glucose and fructose are isomers.

items.p: Two different sugars both have the formula C₆H₁₂O₆. What does a formula leave out?
items.a: A formula leaves out how the atoms are arranged. The two sugars have the same atoms, joined in different arrangements.
items.why: A strong answer says that the count of atoms is the same and the arrangement differs.

items.p: Many people think salt is made of tiny NaCl molecules. Explain what is wrong with this idea.
items.a: Salt is a crystal. Sodium and chlorine atoms alternate in every direction, and each sodium has six chlorine neighbours. No sodium belongs to one chlorine alone. The formula gives the ratio, one to one.
items.why: A strong answer describes the repeating pattern and says that the formula is a ratio.

items.p: Hydrogen gas burns. Water puts fires out. How can water be made partly of hydrogen?
items.a: In water the atoms are joined into new molecules, H₂O. A compound behaves like itself. It does not behave like the elements it is made from.
items.why: A strong answer says that joining atoms makes a new substance with its own behaviour.

items.p: Plan a test: does twice the baking soda need twice the vinegar before the fizzing stops?
items.a: Put 1 level teaspoon of baking soda in one glass and 2 in another. Add vinegar one teaspoon at a time and count until the fizzing stops. Keep the spoon, the vinegar and the stirring the same.
items.why: A strong answer changes only the amount of baking soda, counts something, and keeps everything else the same.

items.p: Is a formula a fact about nature, or a tool that people made?

views.says: It is a fact. Water has two hydrogen atoms for each oxygen atom, and anyone who measures will find that.
It is a tool. A formula sums up many measurements. We should not mistake our summary for the thing itself.
It is both. The letters are ours, and the numbers belong to the water.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. One reason is that the drop counts in Count the Drops could not be chosen. Another is that the letters could have been different, and that a formula leaves out the arrangement of the atoms.
items.why: Scientists and philosophers still discuss this. A strong answer separates the part of a formula that was agreed from the part that was measured.

items.p: Draw a flat piece of a salt crystal: 3 rows of 3 atoms, in two colours. Neighbours side by side must differ.
items.a: A 3 by 3 grid of circles coloured like a chessboard. There are 5 circles of one colour and 4 of the other.
items.why: A strong drawing alternates the colours along every row and every column. In a real grain the two kinds are equal in number, because the pattern goes on for millions of rows.
items.art: A blank 3 by 3 grid of empty circles.

quiz.why: The small 2 follows the H, so it counts hydrogen atoms. The O has no number, so there is one oxygen atom.

quiz.p: How many oxygen atoms are there in one molecule of CO₂?
quiz.why: The small 2 follows the O, so there are two oxygen atoms. There is one carbon atom.

quiz.p: CO and CO₂ are made of the same two elements. Are they the same substance?
opts: No. The number of oxygen atoms differs.
Yes. The elements are the same.
No. CO has no carbon in it.

quiz.p: What does the formula NaCl say about a grain of salt?

Only two atoms in the whole grain

quiz.why: Salt is a crystal with no separate molecules. Its formula gives the ratio, one sodium for every chlorine.

quiz.p: Why does twice as much lemon juice clear about twice as much iodine?
opts: Their molecules react in fixed counts
quiz.why: One vitamin C molecule in the juice changes one iodine molecule. So the amounts go up together.

quiz.p: Salt has different names in different languages, but one formula.
quiz.why: True. Uppu, namak and nun are everyday names. The formula NaCl is the same in every country.

quiz.p: Which name tells you the most about what a substance is made of?
quiz.why: A chemical name contains the names of the elements. Sodium chloride holds sodium and chlorine.

quiz.p: Two substances have the same formula. What can still be different?
quiz.why: A formula gives the kinds of atoms and the numbers. It leaves out the arrangement. Glucose and fructose are an example.

quiz.p: Which of these can heated salt, NaCl, never give off?
quiz.why: Water needs hydrogen and oxygen atoms. Salt has only sodium and chlorine, and heating cannot make new kinds of atoms.

quiz.p: People chose the 2 in H₂O, just as they chose the letter H.
quiz.why: False. The letter was agreed by people. The 2 was found by measuring the gases that water is made from.

quiz.p: Which of these substances has only one kind of atom?
quiz.why: O₂ has only oxygen atoms, so it is an element. The others have two different symbols, so they are compounds.

maths.problem: In Atom Market you build water, H₂O, from atom cards. How many H cards and how many O cards do you need to build 5 water molecules? How many cards is that in all?
maths.answer: 10 H cards and 5 O cards, which is 15 cards.
maths.explain: Each water molecule needs 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom. 5 times 2 is 10, and 5 times 1 is 5. 10 and 5 make 15.
maths.context: In the game Atom Market each card is one atom. You lay down the right cards to build a formula.
maths.why_maths: A formula is a recipe for one molecule. Multiplying tells you what many molecules need.

maths.problem: In Count the Drops, 1 teaspoon of lemon juice cleared 6 drops of iodine. 2 teaspoons cleared 11 drops, and 3 teaspoons cleared 17. About how many drops would 5 teaspoons clear? Explain how you decided.
maths.explain: Each extra teaspoon cleared 5 or 6 more drops. 3 teaspoons cleared 17. Two more teaspoons add about 11 or 12. 17 and 11 make 28, and 17 and 12 make 29.
maths.context: In Count the Drops you add iodine drop by drop to glasses of lemon juice. These are made-up counts for 1, 2 and 3 teaspoons of juice.
maths.why_maths: When two amounts go up together in equal steps, you can predict a glass you have not tested.

maths.problem: Here are three counts from Count the Drops. 1 teaspoon of lemon juice cleared 6 drops, 2 teaspoons cleared 7 and 3 teaspoons cleared 17. Which count looks wrong? What would you do about it?
maths.answer: The 7 drops for 2 teaspoons looks wrong. Make that glass again and count once more.
maths.explain: From 1 to 3 teaspoons the count rose by 11, so each teaspoon adds 5 or 6 drops. The middle glass should be near 11 or 12. A count of 7 fits no pattern. The likeliest causes are a missed stir or a wrong spoonful.
maths.context: In Count the Drops you count how many drops of iodine each glass of lemon juice clears. These are made-up counts with one odd result.
maths.why_maths: A pattern in the numbers shows which result to doubt and test again.

maths.problem: In Dough Atoms you built a salt block of 8 balls, with 4 of each colour. A bigger block has 3 balls along each edge, and the colours still take turns. How many balls does it have? Can the two colours be equal?
maths.answer: 27 balls. The colours cannot be equal. There are 14 of one colour and 13 of the other.
maths.explain: 3 times 3 times 3 is 27. An odd number cannot be split into two equal whole numbers. A block with 4 balls along each edge has 64 balls, 32 of each. A real grain has millions of atoms along each edge, so one extra atom makes no difference.
maths.context: In Dough Atoms you build a small block of salt from dough balls in two colours that take turns.
maths.why_maths: Counting a small model shows why the formula of salt is a ratio. It also shows why the ratio fits a real grain.

maths.problem: In the Name Collector you wrote the formula of table sugar, C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁. How many atoms are in one molecule? Now look only at the H and the O. How many water molecules could those atoms make?
maths.answer: 45 atoms. The hydrogen and oxygen atoms could make exactly 11 water molecules.
maths.explain: 12 and 22 and 11 make 45. Each water molecule needs 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom. 22 divided by 2 is 11, and there are 11 oxygen atoms, so none is left over. Sugar has the atoms of 12 carbons and 11 waters. That is why sugars are called carbohydrates.
maths.context: In the Name Collector you write the everyday names, the chemical name and the formula of four kitchen substances. One of them is table sugar.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the atoms in a formula into groups can show a pattern that the formula hides.

maths.problem: In Water from a Dry Powder, heat changes two units of baking soda, NaHCO₃, into three things. They are one unit of washing soda, Na₂CO₃, one water molecule, H₂O, and one carbon dioxide molecule, CO₂. Count each kind of atom before and after. Is any atom lost?
maths.answer: No atom is lost. Before and after there are 2 sodium, 2 hydrogen, 2 carbon and 6 oxygen atoms.
maths.explain: Two units of NaHCO₃ have 2 sodium, 2 hydrogen, 2 carbon and 6 oxygen atoms. Na₂CO₃ has 2 sodium, 1 carbon and 3 oxygen. H₂O has 2 hydrogen and 1 oxygen. CO₂ has 1 carbon and 2 oxygen. The oxygen adds up to 3 and 1 and 2, which is 6.
maths.context: In Water from a Dry Powder a grown-up heats baking soda, and water collects on a cold plate. Heat rearranges the atoms of the baking soda into three new substances.
maths.why_maths: Counting atoms on both sides checks that a change only rearranged atoms and made none.

how_we_found_out.story: Two hundred years ago, chemists had no shared way to write a substance. Alchemists had drawn secret pictures, and each country used its own names. In 1808 John Dalton, a teacher in Manchester, drew each kind of atom as a circle with a mark inside. He also guessed how atoms join. He thought nature would choose the simplest way. So he wrote water as one hydrogen atom joined to one oxygen atom. Measurements did not agree. In 1805 Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and Alexander von Humboldt had measured the gases that form water. Two measures of hydrogen joined with one of oxygen. In 1811 Amedeo Avogadro explained what this meant. Water must hold two hydrogen atoms for each oxygen atom. Few chemists listened to him. In 1813 the Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius proposed letters in place of circles. A number showed how many atoms there were. Dalton disliked the letters all his life. For fifty years some chemists wrote water as HO and others as H₂O. In 1860, at a meeting in Karlsruhe, Stanislao Cannizzaro argued that Avogadro had been right. In the years after, chemists came to agree on H₂O.
how_we_found_out.who: John Dalton in England, Gay-Lussac and Humboldt in France, Avogadro and Cannizzaro in Italy, and Jöns Jacob Berzelius in Sweden
how_we_found_out.when: Gay-Lussac and Humboldt measured the gases in 1805. Dalton's circles were printed in 1808. Avogadro wrote in 1811, and Berzelius proposed letters in 1813. The meeting in Karlsruhe was in 1860.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That water is HO, one hydrogen atom joined to one oxygen atom. Dalton chose this because it was the simplest. The measured gases, two measures of hydrogen to one of oxygen, showed that water is H₂O.
how_we_found_out.art: An old page with John Dalton's circle symbols for hydrogen, oxygen and water on the left, and the letters H₂O written in ink on the right.

roots.context: In this unit you read formulas such as H₂O and NaCl. You also counted drops to see why their numbers are fixed. Here we ask which part of a formula comes from people and which part comes from the substance.

deep_truth.truth: In Count the Drops, twice as much lemon juice cleared about twice as many drops of iodine. Nobody chose that number, and you found it by counting. People chose the letters H and O for water, but they had to measure to find the 2. So the letters in a formula are an agreement, and the small numbers are discoveries.
deep_truth.habit: We treat a formula as one thing, either as a fact of nature or as a label. It is two things written together. The symbols could have been different. The numbers could not.
deep_truth.evidence: In Count the Drops the counts rose in equal steps, whatever anyone guessed beforehand. Dalton wrote water as HO, and measurements of the two gases made chemists change it to H₂O. The letters were proposed by Berzelius in 1813, in place of Dalton's circles.

three.who_am_i: About 99 of every 100 atoms in your body are hydrogen, oxygen, carbon or nitrogen. Your body is written with the same few symbols as the sea and the air.
three.what_is_life: A mango tree builds sugar from CO₂ and H₂O. You eat the sugar and breathe out CO₂ and H₂O. The same atoms pass from one living being to the next.
three.what_is_this_world: People call water by thousands of names. The water has two hydrogen atoms for each oxygen atom, whatever anyone calls it.

roots.thread: People have given salt hundreds of names, and each name belongs to one language. The formula NaCl belongs to no language, and a chemist anywhere can read it. With 118 symbols, people can write every substance yet found: a rock, a river, the air, a mango and a child. Many sages taught that the many things of the world come from one source. The science here says something close and plain. All the substances we know are built from about ninety kinds of atoms, joined in different numbers.

Count the Drops (core) needs 3 or 4 lemons, povidone-iodine solution, flour and clear glasses. The number of drops depends on the lemons and on the strength of the bottle. One teaspoon of juice may clear anything from 4 to 15 drops. The steps say what to do if the count is very low or very high. The end point is hard to judge to within 1 or 2 drops. Expect 2 teaspoons to clear about twice as many drops as 1 teaspoon. Expect 3 teaspoons to clear about three times as many. Iodine stains cloth, and lemon juice takes the stain out. Water from a Dry Powder is outside the core path, because a grown-up must heat a pan on the stove. A gas flame makes water of its own. So the plate must sit on the pan like a lid, and only its middle is read. Damp salt can mist the plate faintly at the first check. Baking soda must be used, and baking powder will not do. The powder left behind is washing soda, which must not be tasted. Dough Atoms (core) needs chapati dough, turmeric and coffee powder. The Name Collector (core) needs only the kitchen jars and the family. Read It Out (core) and Atom Market are played with the printed cards, and both work with two players or one. Clues Inside a Name depends on the packets at home, and ingredient lists differ from brand to brand. No part needs a garden or an animal.
